title: Check the web address first

cards.text: CISA says odd or incorrect web addresses can be warning signs. A misspelling alone does not prove a site is fake.
cards.line: Read it slowly, letter by letter.

cards.text: The FTC says to use a phone number or website you know is real when you contact a company. Do not trust a link just because it looks familiar.
cards.line: Use a path you know when you can.

cards.text: CISA says to type the address yourself if you are sure you know it. This gives you time to check each letter.
cards.line: Your own typing gives you time to check.

checks.prompt: A web address has a strange spelling. What should you do?
checks.why: CISA lists incorrect links, like amaz a n.com, as a common sign of a fake message.

checks.prompt: A link in a message looks odd. What is safer?
options: Leave it and type the known address
Open it in a new tab
Reply and ask if it is real
checks.answer: Leave it and type the known address
checks.why: CISA says to type the address yourself if you are sure you know it.

checks.prompt: A message links to your bank. What should you use?
options: Call the number in the message
checks.why: The FTC says to use a website you know is real when you contact a company.

takeaway: Check the spelling, then type a web address you already know.

situations.text: A web address has a strange spelling. Does that alone prove the site is fake?
situations.why: A misspelling alone does not prove a site is fake, but check each letter.

situations.text: A link in a message looks odd, so you type the address you already know yourself.
situations.why: CISA says to type the address yourself if you are sure you know it.

situations.text: A link can look familiar and still lead to a fake site.
situations.why: The FTC says not to trust a link just because it looks familiar.
